evidence: Cic. Sen. 17: ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī
terms.comment: Cicero’s helmsman sits still at the stern while the young crew climb the masts and run along the gangways. To a girl, Quiēta sedē; to several, Quiētī sedēte.
In Terence it calms someone down: easy, keep quiet. To a child who will not keep still, settle down.

evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.55: vidēmus igitur ut conquiēscere nē īnfantēs quidem possint

phrases.latin: cum aliī mālōs scandant, aliī per forōs cursent, aliī sentīnam exhauriant, ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī
phrases.english: while some climb the masts, others run up and down the gangways, others bail out the bilge, he sits still at the stern holding the tiller

phrases.latin: vidēmus igitur ut conquiēscere nē īnfantēs quidem possint
phrases.english: so we see that not even babies can keep still

phrases.latin: Quiētus sedē, dum cēnāmus; posteā lūdēs.
phrases.english: Sit still while we have dinner; you can play afterwards.

sources: Lewis & Short: quiesco · Lewis & Short: conquiesco · Lewis & Short: sedeo
